The Home Depot · Price Adjustments

A routine discount had become a workaround.

Associates had workarounds for competitor matches and damaged-item discounts. I designed a markdown path in Order Up that kept the order visible and approval rules explicit.

Role
Staff UX Designer
Scope
Discovery across 12 stores, markdown interactions, and usability testing
Key decision
A fly-out preserves cart context while an associate applies a markdown
Outcome
A 50-store pilot followed by chain-wide rollout; reported impact remains directional

I — Inspiration

Reason codes didn’t cover what happened on the floor

On the store floor, a competitor match or a damaged item was an ordinary reason to change a price. In the software, associates had to find their own way through it. The opportunity was to bring that everyday judgment into the product without losing the controls the business needed.

A competitor match or damaged-item discount was a routine request, but Order Up did not give associates a consistent way to handle it. Workarounds lengthened transactions, and the official reason codes did not cover the situations on the floor.

Observation and interviews across 12 stores showed that managers trusted associates to make good calls. The product needed to support that judgment without discarding the business controls.

Operations partners defined the constraints: adjustments over $50 needed manager approval, each store had a satisfaction budget, and order-level markdowns had to allocate across SKUs. Transaction time mattered to the business.

D — Design Process

Testing favored a fly-out that kept the order visible

I iterated item-level and order-level concepts, then tested task completion, transaction time, and perceived usability. Associates needed the order visible while multitasking across apps and explaining the discount math to customers. “Markdown” was more familiar than “adjustment.”

The fly-out performed best on task completion and perceived usability. I developed it into apply, update, and remove paths, with the order summary showing the discount and the approval requirement remaining explicit.

E — Engagement

Keep associate judgment and business controls together

Operations partners supplied the rules the interaction had to preserve: manager approval above $50, a store satisfaction budget, and allocation across SKUs for an order-level markdown. Those constraints were part of the experience, not details to append after the interface was chosen.

Observation showed that managers trusted associates to make sound calls. I connected that finding to a workflow in which the associate could see the order and explain the discount while working. The product could support judgment and maintain approval requirements in the same interaction.

A — Action

Keep the calculation beside the conversation

I developed apply, update, and remove paths for item-level and order-level markdowns. The order summary kept the discount visible while the approval rule remained explicit. This made the familiar store task a consistent product path, with the same context available as an associate explained it to a customer.

S — Success

From a 50-store pilot to chain-wide rollout

The markdown feature was piloted in 50 stores, then rolled out to all Home Depot stores. The project presentation reports lower transaction times, reduced shrink, stronger standard-procedure adoption, and associates feeling more empowered at 30, 60, and 90 days after launch.

These retrospective trends are directional; no numerical magnitudes are available, and they have not been independently revalidated.

My takeaway: preserving order context and using the associate’s terminology made the approval rules easier to work within. Flexibility and business controls belonged in the same workflow.

I’m happy to walk through the prototypes, testing, and approval constraints.
